## Data

We begin by loading the data necessary for this analysis

### Clean data

The data for the five sites is provided as a simple text file in CSV format. Each file contains the dates of the peak bloom of the cherry trees at the respective site, alongside the geographical location of the site. The six columns in each data file are:
- `location`: a human-readable location identifier (`string`).
- `lat`: (approximate) latitude of the cherry trees (`double`).
- `long`: (approximate) longitude of the cherry trees (`double`).
- `alt`: (approximate) altitude of the cherry trees (`double`).
- `year`: year of the observation (`integer`).
- `bloom_date`: date of peak bloom of the cherry trees ([ISO 8601](https://xkcd.com/1179/) date `string`). The "peak bloom date" may be defined differently for different sites
- `bloom_doy`: days since January 1st until peak bloom (`integer`). January 1st is `1`.

#### Kyoto

The file `kyoto.csv` has been obtained from Yasuyuki Aono (`aono(at)envi.osakafu-u.ac.jp`) at <http://atmenv.envi.osakafu-u.ac.jp/aono/kyophenotemp4/>.

The geographical location at `35.01198°N` (latitude), `135.6761°E` (longitude), `44` meters above sea levels (altitude) roughly corresponds to the **Nakanoshima** area of the **Arashiyama Park** in Kyoto, Japan.

The peak bloom date of the **Prunus jamasakura (Japanese mountain cherry)** is determined by a local news paper in Arashiyama (Kyoto, Japan). Data prior to 1888 is extracted from various descriptions or estimated:
- Data from the 9th to the 14th centuries was acquired and analyzed by Aono and Saito (2010; International Journal of Biometeorology, 54, 211-219).
- Phenology for 15th to 21st centuries was acquired and analyzed by Aono and Kazui (2008; International Journal of Climatology, 28, 905-914).

Note that the data set for Kyoto includes implicit missing values (`NA`s). [Chapter 18 "Missing Values"](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/missing-values) of Hadley Wickham's book "R for Data Science (2e)" describes strategies for dealing with implicit `NA`s.

```{r}
#| label: load-kyoto
#| output: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

kyoto <- read_csv("data/kyoto.csv") |> 
  complete(year = full_seq(year, 1), location) |> 
  mutate(country = "japan") |> 
  fill(location, lat, long, alt, .direction = "downup")
```

Plot the time series for Kyoto

```{r}
#| label: fig-kyoto
#| fig-cap: "Peak cherry blossom days in Kyoto, Japan"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

fig_kyoto <- kyoto |> 
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = year, y = bloom_doy)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, colour = "#644128", se = TRUE) +
  geom_step(linetype = "dotted", colour = "#a53860", lwd = 0.5) +
  geom_point(color = "#ff0054", alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(seq(800, 2000, by = 100), NA)) +
  labs(
    title = "Peak cherry blossom days in Kyoto, Japan", 
    subtitle = "Cultivar: Prunus jamasakura (Japanese mountain cherry)",
    x = NULL, y = NULL,
    caption = "Source: Yasuyuki Aono"
  ) +
  theme_light()

print(fig_kyoto)

ggsave(filename = "figures/fig_kyoto.png", plot = fig_kyoto, bg = "white")
```

Here we have used **locally estimated scatterplot smoothing (LOESS)** or **locally weighted scatterplot smoothing (LOWESS)** to highlight how the average peak bloom day changed over the years. 

We could explicitly model this with a **local level (+ trend)** state-space model that we fit with the **Kalman filter and Smoother**, which also allows us to effectively deal with **missing observations**.

MeteoSwiss suggests using a **Gaussian Kernel** with a *20-year window* to extract the trend, which is equivalent to using a **low-pass filter** that shuts down all higher frequencies.

It also looks like the observations exhibit **heteroskedasticity**, that is, the variance changes over time, and it looks like the variance has become more narrow over time.

We can use **changepoint detection** methods to test for the changing time trend and the changing variance.

Assuming that the data in the past is correct, there do seem to be seasonal cycles, perhaps connected to solar activity or the tilt of the earth.

There is a clear trend towards earlier blooming, perhaps connected to anthropogenic climate change and urbanization. Studies attribute about half of the earlier blooming times in recent years to the **urban heat island effect**, and the other half to **climate change**.

Modelling the local level and the trend would be useful if we are to forecast a couple years into the future, since an individual prediction may be incorrect, but on average, they may be good. 

However, since we are only interested in forecasting a single moment in time, which may be greatly influenced by local weather, we probably are better off using historical weather data that we augment with forecasts, either by professional forecasters or by extrapolating the previous predictors.

#### Liestal

The file `liestal.csv` contains observations for **a single wild cherry (prunus avium) tree** in **Liestal-Weideli**, at `7.4814°N` (latitude), `7.730519°E` (longitude) and `350` meters above sea levels (altitude). 

```{r}
#| label: load-liestal
#| output: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

liestal <- read_csv("data/liestal.csv") |> 
  mutate(country = "switzerland")
```

The **peak bloom date** is defined as the day when **25%** of the blossoms are in full bloom. The date is determined by [MeteoSwiss](https://www.meteoswiss.admin.ch/climate/climate-change/vegetation-development/long-term-series-of-phenological-observations.html). This means that 70% of buds would be open a some days later. This raises the question of whether we should model the locations separately.

The data is provided by **Landwirtschaftliches Zentrum Ebenrain, Sissach and MeteoSwiss**.

Let's plot the time series for Liestal, Switzerland:

```{r}
#| label: fig-liestal
#| fig-cap: "Peak cherry blossom days for Liestal-Weideli, Switzerland"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

fig_liestal <- liestal |> 
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = year, y = bloom_doy)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, colour = "#644128", se = TRUE) +
  geom_step(linetype = "dotted", colour = "#a53860", lwd = 0.75) +
  geom_point(color = "#ff0054", alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(seq(1880, 2020, by = 20), NA)) +
  labs(
    title = "Peak cherry blossom days for Liestal-Weideli, Switzerland",
    subtitle = "Cultivar: Wild cherry (prunus avium)",
    x = NULL, y = NULL,
    caption = "Source: Landwirtschaftliches Zentrum Ebenrain, Sissach and MeteoSwiss"
  ) +
  theme_light()

print(fig_liestal)

ggsave(filename = "figures/fig_liestal.png", plot = fig_liestal, bg = "white")
```

For Liestal you can see the impact of the infamous heat summer of 2003 which I remember from my childhood, although interestingly, there's another record in 1990.

#### New York

The file `newyorkcity.csv` contains **only a single observation** for the year 2024. It concerns the **Yoshino cherry (prunus × yedoensis)** tree in **Washington Square Park**, New York City, at `40.7304 °N` (latitude), `-73.99809°E` (longitude) and `8.5` meters above sea level (altitude).

```{r}
#| label: load-newyorkcity
#| output: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

newyorkcity <- read_csv("data/nyc.csv") |> 
  mutate(country = "unitedstates")
```

Luckily, there are some historical observations dating *back to 2019* in the data provided by **USA-NPN**. The Washington Square Park has site id `32789` and the **Yoshino** cherry you should predict has species id `228`.

```{r}
#| label: load-historical-data-nyc
#| output: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

nyc_data_npn <- read_csv("data/USA-NPN_status_intensity_observations_data.csv") |> 
  filter(Site_ID == 32789, Species_ID == 228) |> 
  mutate(Observation_Date = mdy(Observation_Date))
```

This file now contains individual observations of the phenophase and not the actual peak bloom date. We use the variable `Intensity_Value` which is either `-9999`, `95% or more`, `Less than 5%`, `25-49%`, `75-94%`, `50-74%`. Since according to the variable `Individual_ID`, only one tree, `183140` is being observed, we can use the first date where `Intensity_Value` is `50-74%` as our `bloom_doy`.

```{r}
#| label: clean-npn-nyc-data
#| warning: true

nyc_data <- nyc_data_npn |>
  arrange(Observation_Date) |>
  mutate(year = year(Observation_Date)) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarize(
    first_flower_index = min(which((Intensity_Value %in% c("75-94%", "95% or more")))),
    bloom_date = as_date(strftime(Observation_Date[first_flower_index], format = "%Y-%m-%d")),
    bloom_doy = Day_of_Year[first_flower_index],
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(bloom_doy)) |>
  select(-first_flower_index) |>
  mutate(country = "unitedstates", location = "newyorkcity") |> 
  arrange(year)
```

Then we combine the data sets. Make sure not to add any dates twice.

```{r}
#| label: augment-nyc-data

newyorkcity <- newyorkcity |>
  bind_rows(nyc_data |> filter(year != 2024)) |>  
  fill(lat, long, alt)
```

We now have a total of four observations for New York City

```{r}
#| label: tbl-nyc-data
#| tbl-cap: "Augmented NYC observations"

newyorkcity |> 
  filter(location == "newyorkcity") |> 
  gt()
```

Plot the time series for New York City, USA

```{r}
#| label: fig-newyorkcity
#| fig-cap: "Peak cherry blossom days for New York City, USA"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

fig_newyorkcity <- newyorkcity |> 
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = year, y = bloom_doy)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, colour = "#644128", se = TRUE) +
  geom_step(linetype = "dotted", colour = "#a53860", lwd = 0.75) +
  geom_point(color = "#ff0054", alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Peak cherry blossom days for New York City, USA", 
    subtitle = "Cultivar: Yoshino cherry (prunus × yedoensis)",
    x = NULL, y = NULL,
    caption = "Source: Geroge Mason University and USA-NPN"
  ) +
  theme_light()

print(fig_newyorkcity)

ggsave(filename = "figures/fig_newyorkcity.png", plot = fig_newyorkcity, bg = "white")
```


#### Vancouver

The file `vancouver.csv` contains observations for cherry trees of the cultivar  **Akebono (daybreak cherry)** in **Maple Grove Park**, Vancouver, BC located approximately at `49.2236916°N` (latitude), `-123.1636251°E` (longitude), `24` meters above sea levels (altitude).

Akebono (daybreak cherry). A medium sized tree growing 8 m × 8 m (25 ft) with a stiff, upright-spreading crown, eventually becoming umbrella shaped. ‘Akebono’ flowers in late March or early April, usually following the purple-leaf plums by about a week. Flowers are produced abundantly, shell-pink fading to nearly white. ‘Akebono’ is a seedling of Prunus yedoensis ‘Somei-yoshino‘(Tokyo cherry) selected in 1925 at a California nursery. ‘Akebono’ is by far the most commonly planted early spring flowering cherry in this area, and is celebrated for its essentially rainproof flowers and freedom from disease. Autumn colour is yellow to pumpkin orange. <https://vcbf.ca/cherry_cultivars/akebono/>.

```{r}
#| label: load-vancouver
#| output: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

vancouver <- read_csv("data/vancouver.csv") |> 
  mutate(country = "canada")
```

Unfortunately, there are **only three observations** for 2022, 2023, and 2024, respectively. But casual observations have been recorded in the form of **photos posted** to the [VCBF Neighbourhood Blog for Kerrisdale](https://forums.botanicalgarden.ubc.ca/threads/kerrisdale.36008/). You can **search the forum** for the keywords `"Akebono"` (i.e., the name of the cultivar) and `"Maple Grove Park"` (i.e., the location of the trees).

After searching through the web forum, I have decided to add the following observations to the data set:

```{r}
#| label: define-vancouver_forum

vancouver_forum <- tribble(
  ~ year, ~ bloom_date,
  2021, "2021-03-31", # Start: 2021-03-21, Full: 2021-03-31, Full: 2021-04-07
  2020, "2020-04-03", # Full bloom
  2018, "2018-03-18", # Full bloom
  2017, "2017-04-11", # Full bloom 
  2015, "2015-03-19", # Full bloom
  2011, "2011-04-01", # Full bloom was over on 2011-04-15
  2010, "2010-03-14", # 60% bloom on 2010-03-07
  2008, "2008-04-14" # Start: 2008-04-06, Full: 2008-04-14, finished: 2008-04-22
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    bloom_date = as_date(bloom_date),
    bloom_doy = as.numeric(1 + as_date(bloom_date) - as_date(paste0(year, "-01-01"))),
    location = "vancouver",
    country = "canada"
  )
```

We can do some additional plausibility checks. For example, spring 2010 was indeed unusually warm, [causing cherry blossoms to bloom during the Vancouver 2010 Winter Olympics](https://www.upi.com/News_Photos/view/upi/33393f9d20159ecb347de9aa1d670922/2010-Winter-Olympics-in-Vancouver/). National Geographic claimed it was the [warmest Olympics to date](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/adventure/article/100212-vancouver-2010-warmest-winter-olympics).

Once we are statsfied with the plausibility, we can add these observations to the data set

```{r}
#| label: augment-vancouver

vancouver <- vancouver |> 
  bind_rows(vancouver_forum) |> 
  fill(lat, long, alt) |> 
  arrange(year)
```

Now we have a total of eleven observations for Vancouver, BC.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-augmented-vancouver-data
#| tbl-cap: "Augmented Vancouver data"

vancouver |> 
  filter(location == "vancouver") |> 
  gt()
```

Plot the data for Vancouver BC, Canada

```{r}
#| label: fig-vancouver
#| fig-cap: "Peak cherry blossom days for Vancouver BC, Canada"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

fig_vancouver <- vancouver |> 
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = year, y = bloom_doy)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, colour = "#644128", se = TRUE) +
  geom_step(linetype = "dotted", colour = "#a53860", lwd = 0.75) +
  geom_point(color = "#ff0054", alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Peak cherry blossom days for Vancouver BC, Canada", 
    subtitle = "Cultivar: Akebono (daybreak cherry)",
    x = NULL, y = NULL,
    caption = "Source: Geroge Mason University and VCBF Neighbourhood Blog"
  ) +
  theme_light()

print(fig_vancouver)

ggsave(filename = "figures/fig_vancouver.png", plot = fig_vancouver, bg = "white")
```


#### Washington

The file `washingtondc.csv` has been obtained from the EPA's Climate Change Indicators in the United States <https://www.epa.gov/climate-indicators/cherry-blossoms>.

```{r}
#| label: load-washingtondc
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| output: false

washingtondc <- read_csv("data/washingtondc.csv") |> 
  mutate(country = "unitedstates")
```

The geographical location at `38.88535°N` (latitude), `-77.03863°E` (longitude) and `0` meters above sea level (altitude) correspond to the location of the [Tidal Basin in Washington, DC](https://www.nps.gov/articles/dctidalbasin.htm).

The peak bloom date is defined as the day when **70%** of the **Yoshino cherry (prunus x yedoensis)** are in full bloom, as determined by the [National Park Service](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/cherryblossom/bloom-watch.htm).

Let's plot the data for Washington D.C

```{r}
#| label: fig-washingtondc
#| fig-cap: "Peak cherry blossom days for Washington DC, USA"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

fig_washingtondc <- washingtondc |> 
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = year, y = bloom_doy)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, colour = "#644128", se = TRUE) +
  geom_step(linetype = "dotted", colour = "#a53860", lwd = 0.75) +
  geom_point(color = "#ff0054", alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(seq(1920, 2020, by = 20), NA)) +
  labs(
    title = "Peak cherry blossom days for Washington DC, USA",
    subtitle = "Cultivar: Yoshino cherry (prunus × yedoensis )",
    x = NULL, y = NULL,
    caption = "Source: Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Climate Change Indicators in the United States"
  ) +
  theme_light()

print(fig_washingtondc)

ggsave(filename = "figures/fig_washingtondc.png", plot = fig_washingtondc, bg = "white")
```

Now that we have loaded the datasets for the five locations, we can combine them into a single CSV file called `cherry.csv`.

```{r}
#| label: combine-cherry-csv
#| eval: false

cherry <- bind_rows(kyoto, liestal, newyorkcity, vancouver, washingtondc) |> 
  relocate(year, location, country, lat, long, alt, bloom_date)

write_csv(cherry, file = "data/cherry.csv")
```

Now we can load the `cherry.csv` file from our `data/` folder

```{r}
#| label: load-cherry-csv
#| output: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

cherry <- read_csv("data/cherry.csv")
```

We can show the last three observation for each location

```{r}
#| label: tbl-01
#| tbl-cap: "latest 3 observations for each location"

cherry |> 
  group_by(country, location) |> 
  slice_tail(n = 3) |> 
  gt()
```

We can visualize the time series for our five main locations next to each other. Notice the use of the `{stringr}` function `str_to_title()` to convert the first letter of the locations to uppercase.

```{r}
#| label: fig-cherries_1880
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: 100%
#| fig-cap: |
#|   Time series of peak bloom of cherry trees since 1880 at five different sites.

df_cherry_1880 <- cherry |> 
  filter(year >= 1880)

fig_cherries <- ggplot(data = df_cherry_1880, aes(year, bloom_doy)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, colour = "#644128", se = FALSE) +
  geom_step(linetype = "dotted", colour = "#ffa5ab") +
  geom_point(color = "#ff0080", alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(seq(1880, 2020, by = 40), NA)) +
  facet_grid(cols = vars(str_to_title(location))) +
  labs(
    title = "Peak bloom (since Jan 1st)",
    x = NULL, 
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_light()

print(fig_cherries)

ggsave(filename = "figures/fig_cherries.png", plot = fig_cherries, bg = "white")
```

Create summary statistics to get an overview over the data. Specifically, we are interested in the range of the `year` variable, the total number of observations at each location, and the mean, median, and standard deviation of the `bloom_doy` variable.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-summary-statistics
#| tbl-cap: "Summary statistics for the main data set"

cherry |> 
  filter(!is.na(bloom_doy)) |> 
  group_by(location) |> 
  summarise(
    min_year = min(year),
    max_year = max(year),
    n_obs = n(),
    mean = round(mean(bloom_doy)),
    median = round(median(bloom_doy)),
    sd = round(sd(bloom_doy))
  ) |> 
  gt()
```

We see that the standard deviation for Liestal is much larger than the rest, where peak bloom dates are on average about a weak apart from their historical average.

We check for missing observations in the most recent years:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-check-kyoto-missing
#| tbl-cap: "The most recent missing values in the Kyoto dataset"

cherry |> 
  filter(location == "kyoto") |> 
  filter(is.na(bloom_doy)) |> 
  tail() |> 
  gt()
```

Kyoto has multiple implicit `NA`s, including in 1730, 1872, 1895, 1919, 1921, and 1945. So if we use data since 1880, as the demo analysis suggests, we still have four `NA`s. For time series analysis, we usually assume equally-spaced observations, and therefore need to either cut the data to start in 1946, or to replace the `NA`s with a sensible value. The other four locations do not contain any implicit `NA`.

Plot the distribution of the peak bloom days for the locations:

```{r}
#| label: fig-histogram
#| fig-cap: "Histogram of peak bloom (since Jan 1st)"

cherry |> 
  filter(year >= 1950) |> 
  filter(!(location %in% c("newyorkcity", "vancouver"))) |> 
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = bloom_doy, fill = location)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  labs(title = "Histogram of peak bloom (since Jan 1st)", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_light() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.title = element_blank())
```

Let's use a density plot instead:

```{r}
#| label: fig-density-plot
#| fig-cap: "Denisty plots of peak bloom (since Jan 1st)"

cherry |> 
  filter(year >= 1950) |> 
  filter(!(location %in% c("newyorkcity", "vancouver"))) |> 
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = bloom_doy, fill = location, colour = location)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "Denisty plots of peak bloom (since Jan 1st)", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_light() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.title = element_blank())
```

Let's plot all five time series in the same plot.

```{r}
#| label: fig-cherry-blossoms-combined
#| fig-cap: "Peak cherry blossom days for different locations"
#| warning: false

fig_combined <- cherry |> 
  filter(year >= 1880) |> 
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = year, y = bloom_doy, colour = location)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE) +
  geom_step(linetype = "dotted", lwd = 0.5) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 2.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(seq(1880, 2020, by = 20), NA)) +
  labs(title = "Peak cherry blossom days by locations", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_light() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.title = element_blank())

print(fig_combined)

ggsave(filename = "figures/fig_combined.png", plot = fig_combined, bg = "white")
```

This graphic highlights the negative linear time trend for all locations.

It also highlights that a linear time trend will likely underestimate the accelerating trend towards earlier peak bloom dates.

A simple method such as **ETS**, which places a lower weight on observations far in the past, may be better at modelling the recent trend.

In the M-comptetitions, a combination of ARIMA, which takes seasonality into account, and ETS, which takes the changing trend into account, usually fared well.

In any case, we should compare all our models against **benchmark models** such as the **naive model**, where the prediction is equal to the last observation, and a simple **AR(1)** model.

### Additional data

The competition organizers provide additional data sets for sites other than the main sites relevant for the competition. We can use these time series in your modeling to help with spatial and temporal extrapolation. For example, we can add predictors to these data sets and train models on additional sites.

#### Japan

The data file `japan.csv` is provided by the [Japanese Meteorological Agency (JMA)](https://www.data.jma.go.jp/sakura/data/) and contains recorded peak bloom dates for cherry trees at various sites across Japan. The sample trees are located within a 5km radius of the location indicated in the data file. 

Load the data set, make implicit missing values explicit and change the `location` variable to only include the city names in lowercase letters.

```{r}
#| label: read-japan
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| output: false

japan <- read_csv("data/japan.csv") |>  
  complete(year =  full_seq(year, 1), location) |> 
  mutate(location = str_remove(location, "Japan/")) |> 
  mutate(location = tolower(location), country = "japan") |> 
  fill(location, lat, long, alt, .direction = "downup") |> 
  mutate(location = factor(location))
```

The `japan.csv` file contains observations between `r min(japan$year)` and `r max(japan$year)` for `r length(unique(japan$location))` locations in Japan.

Select some locations in Japan with altitudes in the range of the five main locations and more than 60 observations. This should hopefully allow us to estimate the effect of altitude on the peak bloom date. Most locations will be close to sea level, which is okay since New York City and Vancouver are at this very low altitude.

```{r}
#| label: select-locations-in-japan
#| warning: false
#| message: false

altitudes <- c(unique(kyoto$alt), unique(liestal$alt), unique(newyorkcity$alt), unique(vancouver$alt), unique(washingtondc$alt))

japan <- japan |>
  group_by(location, lat, long, alt) |> 
  filter(alt %in% seq(min(altitudes) - 10, max(altitudes) + 10)) |> 
  filter(sum(!is.na(bloom_doy)) >= 60) |> 
  ungroup()
```

Let's plot peak bloom dates for selected locations in Japan

```{r}
    subtitle = NULL,

  ) +

print(fig_japan)

ggsave(filename = "figures/fig_japan.png", plot = fig_japan, bg = "white")
```

#### Korea

The file `south_korea.csv` contains **first flowering dates** of cherry trees at various sites across South Korea, curated by the **Korean Meteorological Administration (KMA)**.

Because these are **first flowering dates**, they are likely to occur earlier than hypothetical full bloom dates would be.

Trees in South Korea were assumed to be of the **Prunus × yedoensis** variety based on previous work (Hur, Ahn, and Shim 2014; Chung et al. 2009) and its frequent occurrence.

Again, we make implicit missing values explicit, and I change the location names to lowercase so that to match the style of the main data set.

```{r}
#| label: load-korea
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| output: false

korea <- read_csv("data/south_korea.csv") |> 
  complete(year =  full_seq(year, 1), location) |> 
  mutate(location = str_remove(location, "South Korea/")) |> 
  mutate(location = tolower(location), country = "korea") |> 
  fill(location, lat, long, alt, .direction = "downup") |> 
  mutate(location = factor(location))
```

The `south_korea.csv` file contains observations between `r min(korea$year)` and `r max(korea$year)` at `r length(unique(korea$location))` locations in South Korea.

The locations in Korea have between 15 and 25 observations. 

```{r}
#| label: select-locations-korea
#| warning: false
#| message: false

korea <- korea |>
  group_by(location, lat, long, alt) |> 
  filter(alt %in% seq(min(altitudes) - 10, max(altitudes) + 10)) |> 
  filter(sum(!is.na(bloom_doy)) >= 15) |> 
  ungroup()
```


Let's plot the first bloom dates for selected locations in Korea

```{r}
#| label: fig-korea
#| fig-cap: "First bloom of selected locations in South Korea"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

fig_korea <- korea |>
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = year, y = bloom_doy)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", colour = "#644128", se = FALSE) +
  geom_step(linetype = "dotted", colour = "#ffa5ab", lwd = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "#f72585", alpha = 0.5, size = 2.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(seq(1980, 2020, by = 5), NA)) +
  facet_wrap(facets = vars(location)) +

    title = "First bloom (since Jan 1st) of selected locations in Korea",

print(fig_korea)

ggsave(filename = "figures/fig_korea.png", plot = fig_korea, bg = "white")
```

#### MeteoSwiss

The data file `meteoswiss.csv` contains peak bloom dates for various sites across Switzerland, obtained from <https://opendata.swiss/en/dataset/phanologische-beobachtungen>.

Note that when you use the `{utils}` function `read.csv()` you need to specify the option `encoding = "UTF-8"` to allow for special characters that are common in the German language.

```{r}
#| label: load-meteoswiss
```

The `meteoswiss.csv` file contains observations between `r min(meteoswiss$year)` and `r max(meteoswiss$year)` at `r length(unique(meteoswiss$location))` locations.

The locations have up to 70 observations, but most are at very high altitudes, much higher than the five main locations. I therefore select two locations which have a similar altitude to Liestal and are in close geographical proximity.

```{r}
#| label: select-locations-meteoswiss

meteoswiss_selected <- meteoswiss |>
  group_by(location, lat, long, alt) |> 
  filter(alt %in% seq(min(altitudes) - 10, max(altitudes) + 10)) |>
```

Plot the data for selected locations in Switzerland. Note that for this data set, peak bloom is defined as **50%** of blossoms being in bloom.

```{r}
  scale_x_continuous(

  ) +

print(fig_meteoswiss)
```

I choose only to use "basel-binningen" and "laufenburg" as these locations are reasonably close to Liestal and hence should enjoy a similar climate, and because they include recent observations. Just for fun, I also want to include the three locations near my hometown of Zurich.

```{r}
#| label: save-select-meteoswiss

binningen <- meteoswiss |> 
  filter(location == "basel-binningen") |>
```

I enhance the dataset of the five main locations with observations from the selected locations in Japan and Switzerland. I do not use data from Korea because the observations are few and the phenological event observed is first bloom and not peak bloom.

```{r}
#| label: enhance-cherry-with-selected-locations
#| warning: false
#| message: false

cherry <- cherry |> 
  mutate(bloom_date = date(bloom_date)) |> 
  bind_rows(
  hakodate,
  kochi,
  kumagaya,
  mito,
  muroran,
  osaka,
  tottori,
  binningen,
  laufenburg,
  albisgutli,
  meteoschweiz,
  witikon
```

## Time trend

We can explore models without external predictors that rely solely on past observations and on time trends.

A simple method to predict peak bloom dates is to fit an **ordinary least-squares (OLS)** regression on the observed years and extrapolate the regression function into future. We want to have a separate line for each location, hence we tell R to estimate *interaction* effects. Note that R will automatically exclude `NA`s from the regression.

We only use data **from 1880** to fit the trends, as prior data may not be as reliable/relevant.

```{r}
#| label: fit-linear-time-trend

cherry_ls <- cherry |> 
  filter(location %in% c("kyoto", "liestal", "newyorkcity", "vancouver", "washingtondc"))

ls_fit <- lm(
  formula = bloom_doy ~ 0 + location + location:year,
  data = cherry_ls, 
  subset = year >= 1880
)
```

This simple linear regression functions suggest a trend toward earlier peak bloom at the sites.

```{r}
#| label: summary-linear-model

summary(ls_fit)
```

Unsurprisingly, neither the intercept nor the time trend are statistically significant for Vancouver and New York City, where we have few observations.

We can compute predictions for both the historical observations and for the current year with the `predict()` function. We first use the `expand_grid()` function to create all possible combinations for the years between 1880 and 2025 and the five locations, so that we have the input variables for both the fitted values for the past years and the prediction for the current year

```{r}
#| label: create-grid

cherry_grid <- expand_grid(location = unique(cherry_ls$location), year = 1880:2025)
```

Then we use these input variables to create both point estimates and 90% confidence intervals with `predict()`

```{r}
#| label: create-predictions

predictions <- predict(
  object = ls_fit, newdata = cherry_grid,
  interval = "prediction", level = 0.9
  ) |> 
  bind_cols(cherry_grid) |> 
  rename(prediction = fit, lower = lwr, upper = upr) |> 
  relocate(year, location)
```

Plot only the fitted values, i.e., the predictions for the actual observations between 2015 and 2024

```{r}
#| label: fig-fitted
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: 100%
#| fig-cap: |
#|   Predictions and 90% prediction intervals from simple linear regression models fitted to
#|   five sites.

cherry_ls |>
  right_join(predictions, by = c("year", "location")) |>
  filter((location == "vancouver" & year >= 2015) | (location != "vancouver" & year >= 2015)) |>
  filter((location == "newyorkcity" & year >= 2019) | (location != "newyorkcity" & year >= 2015)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = prediction, ymin = lower, ymax = upper)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_ribbon(color = "black", linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.8, fill = NA) +
  geom_point(aes(y = bloom_doy)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2015, 2018, 2021, 2024)) +
  facet_grid(cols = vars(str_to_title(location))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Peak bloom (days since Jan 1st)") +
  theme_light()
```

We see that the slope of the time trend has become steeper since 2015. If we assume that this trend continues, our prediction for the current year will be too high.

We create a function called `day_to_date()` that converts `bloom_doy` into an ISO date

```{r}
#| label: day_to_date

#' Small helper function to convert the day of year to the actual date.
#'
#' @param year year as an integer
#' @param doy day of the year as integer (1 means January 1st)
#' @return date string

doy_to_date <- function(year, doy) {
  strptime(paste(year, doy, sep = "-"), "%Y-%j") |> # create date object
    strftime("%Y-%m-%d") # translate back to date string in ISO 8601 format
}
```


Based on this simple model, the peak bloom dates at these sites in 2025 are predicted to occur on.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-predictions
#| tbl-cap: "Predicted peak bloom dates at the four sites"

predictions |>
  filter(year == 2025) |>
  mutate(across(c(prediction, lower, upper), round)) |> 
  mutate(prediction_date = doy_to_date(year, prediction)) |> 
  relocate(year, location, prediction_date) |> 
  gt()
```

### Averaging

We have only a few observations for Vancouver, BC and for New York City. Although the climate in Vancouver and NYC is different from the other locations, the simplest way to borrow information from the other locations is to average across these three sites.

Hence, we want to fit a straight line through the peak bloom dates, ignoring the actual site. That is, we fit a simple linear time trend on all available observations, but we want to use larger **weights** for observations from the target sites.

#### Vancouver

To run **weighted least squares (WLS)**, the `weights` inside `stats::lm()` argument must be a vector of the same length as the input data and we can use the names of the `location` column to create it. 

We could have created a new variable explicitly with:

```{r}
#| eval: false

cherry$weight <- (cherry_ls$location == "vancouver") + 0.2 * (cherry_ls$location != "vancouver")

cherry$weight <- NULL
```

So the weight put on observations from Vancouver are while observations from other locations receive a weight of only one fifth.

```{r}
#| label: fit-wls-vancouver

ls_fit_for_van <- lm(
  formula = bloom_doy ~ year,
  data = cherry_ls, subset = year >= 1880,
  weights = (location == "vancouver") + 0.2 * (location != "vancouver")
)
```

Create a grid with the input variables for Vancouver only

```{r}
#| label: grid-vancouver

vancouver_grid <- tibble(location = "vancouver", year = 2008:2025)
```

Then we use these inputs to create predictions for Vancouver, 

```{r}
#| label: predict-vancouver

predictions_vancouver <- predict(
  object = ls_fit_for_van, newdata = vancouver_grid,
  interval = "prediction", level = 0.9
  ) |> 
  bind_cols(vancouver_grid) |> 
  rename(prediction = fit, lower = lwr, upper = upr) |> 
  mutate(across(c(prediction, lower, upper), round)) |> 
  mutate(prediction_date = doy_to_date(year, prediction)) |> 
  relocate(year, location, prediction_date)
```

Not surprisingly, the predicted peak bloom dates for Vancouver are now very similar to the other 3 sites:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-predictions-vancouver
#| tbl-cap: "Predictions for Vancouver"

predictions_vancouver |> 
  gt()
```

Due to **rounding** and the **slope** of the time trend being very flat for such a long time series, the predictions are almost the same for every year.

We can plot the fitted values against the actual data from previous years

```{r}
#| label: fig-fitted-vancouver
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: 100%
#| fig-cap: |
#|   Predictions and 90% prediction intervals from a simple linear regression model for Vancouver using data from all four sites.

cherry_ls |>
  right_join(y = predictions_vancouver, by = c("year", "location")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = prediction, ymin = lower, ymax = upper)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_ribbon(color = "black", linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.8, fill = NA) +
  geom_point(aes(y = bloom_doy)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2008:2025) +
  facet_grid(cols = vars(str_to_title(location))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Peak bloom (days since Jan 1st)") +
  theme_light()
```

We see that without including weather data, we are not able to capture the unusually warm springs in Vancouver, such as the one from 2010.

We have made this very cautious prediction since we don't know much about the conditions in Vancouver.

If we were satisfied with these weighted predictions for Vancouver, we could use them to replace the predictions that were made using only data from Vancouver.

```{r}
#| label: replace-vancouver-predictions

predictions <- predictions |>
  filter(location != "vancouver") |>
  bind_rows(predictions_vancouver)
```

#### New York

We once again fit a model on the whole data set, weighting observations from New York City with one and observations from other locations with one fifth.

```{r}
#| label: wls-for-nyc

ls_fit_for_nyc <- lm(
  formula = bloom_doy ~ year,
  data = cherry_ls, subset = year >= 1880,
  weights = (location == "newyorkcity") + 0.2 * (location != "newyorkcity")
)
```

Add inputs since 2019 and the current year

```{r}
#| label: grid-nyc

nyc_grid <- tibble(location = "newyorkcity", year = 2019:2025)
```

Create the fitted values for NYC

```{r}
#| label: fitted-nyc

predictions_nyc <- predict(
  object = ls_fit_for_nyc, newdata = nyc_grid,
  interval = "prediction", level = 0.9
  ) |> 
  bind_cols(nyc_grid) |> 
  rename(prediction = fit, lower = lwr, upper = upr) |> 
  mutate(across(c(prediction, lower, upper), round)) |> 
  mutate(prediction_date = doy_to_date(year, prediction)) |> 
  relocate(year, location, prediction_date)
```

Show the fitted values for New York City

```{r}
#| label: tbl-predictions-nyc
#| tbl-cap: "Predictions for New York City"

predictions_nyc |> 
  gt()
```

Due to rounding, and because the slope of the linear time trend being very flat for such a long time series, the predictions are the same for every year.

We plot the fitted values for New York City and the actual observations

```{r}
#| label: fig-fitted-nyc
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: 100%
#| fig-cap: |
#|   Predictions and 90% prediction intervals from a simple linear regression model for NYC using data from all five sites.

cherry_ls |>
  right_join(predictions_nyc, by = c("year", "location")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = prediction, ymin = lower, ymax = upper)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_ribbon(color = "black", linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.8, fill = NA) +
  geom_point(aes(y = bloom_doy)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2019:2024) +
  facet_grid(cols = vars(str_to_title(location))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Peak bloom (days since Jan 1st)") +
  theme_light()
```

Again, this model does not capture the steepness of the slope of the time trend accurately.

If we were satisfied with the averaged predictions we could replace the predictions that were made using only data from New York City

```{r}
#| label: replace-nyc-predictions

predictions <- predictions |>
  filter(location != "newyorkcity") |>
  bind_rows(predictions_nyc)
```

## Predictors

We have seen that a linear time trend alone is not sufficient to explain the variance in the peak bloom times. It therefore makes sense to include external data on local weather conditions in our model. 

### POWER

We use the `{nasapower}` package described at <https://docs.ropensci.org/nasapower/> to access the [NASA Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources (POWER) API](https://power.larc.nasa.gov/). We create a custom function called `get_power()` to repeatedly query the API with the `nasapower::get_power()` function.

```{r}
#| label: get_power

get_power <- function(
    vars, 
    start = "1981-01-01", 
    end = as.character(Sys.Date()), 
    freq = "daily", 
    lat, long
  ) {
  power <- map2(
    .x  = long,
    .y = lat,
    .f = function(long = .x, lat = .y) {
      res <- nasapower::get_power(
        community = "ag",
        lonlat = c(long, lat),
        pars = vars,
        dates = c(start, end),
        temporal_api = freq
        )
      return(res)
      }
    ) |>
    list_rbind()
  return(power)
}
```


We load the following variables:

- `T2M`: Temperature at 2 Meters. The average air (dry bulb) temperature at 2 meters above the surface of the earth.

- `T2M_MAX:` Temperature at 2 Meters Maximum. The maximum hourly air (dry bulb) temperature at 2 meters above the surface of the earth in the period of interest.

- `T2M_MIN`: Temperature at 2 Meters Minimum. The minimum hourly air (dry bulb) temperature at 2 meters above the surface of the earth in the period of interest.

- `PRECTOTCORR`: Precipitation Corrected. The average MERRA-2 bias corrected total precipitation at the surface of the earth.

- `RH2M`: Relative Humidity at 2 Meters. The ratio of vapor pressure to the saturation vapor pressure with respect to a plane surface of pure water, expressed in percent.

- `PS`: Surface pressure (kPa)

- `WS10M`: Wind Speed at 10 Meters. The average of wind speed at 10 meters above the surface of the earth.

```{r}
#| label: specify-vars

vars <- c(
  "T2M",
  "T2M_MAX",
  "T2M_MIN",
  "PRECTOTCORR",
  "RH2M",
  "PS",
  "WS10M"
)
```

We retrieve the **coordinates** which we will use to match to the nearest weather stations

```{r}
#| label: get-coordinates

crd_kyoto        <- distinct(kyoto, location, country, lat, long)
crd_liestal      <- distinct(liestal, location, country, lat, long)
crd_nyc          <- distinct(newyorkcity, location, country, lat, long)
crd_vancouver    <- distinct(vancouver, location, country, lat, long)
crd_washingtondc <- distinct(washingtondc, location, country, lat, long)

crd_hakodate     <- distinct(hakodate, location, country, lat, long)
crd_kochi        <- distinct(kochi, location, country, lat, long)
crd_kumagaya     <- distinct(kumagaya, location, country, lat, long)
crd_mito         <- distinct(mito, location, country, lat, long)
crd_muroran      <- distinct(muroran, location, country, lat, long)
crd_osaka        <- distinct(osaka, location, country, lat, long)
crd_tottori      <- distinct(tottori, location, country, lat, long)

crd_binningen    <- distinct(binningen, location, country, lat, long)
crd_laufenburg   <- distinct(laufenburg, location, country, lat, long)
crd_albisgutli   <- distinct(albisgutli, location, country, lat, long)
crd_meteoschweiz <- distinct(meteoschweiz, location, country, lat, long)
crd_witikon      <- distinct(witikon, location, country, lat, long)
```

Load the predictors for the locations

```{r}
#| label: load-main-nasa-power
#| eval: false

# Five main locations
power_kyoto <- get_power(vars, lat = crd_kyoto$lat, long = crd_kyoto$long) |> 
  mutate(location = "kyoto", country = "japan")

power_liestal <- get_power(vars, lat = crd_liestal$lat, long = crd_liestal$long) |> 
  mutate(location = "liestal", country = "switzerland")

power_nyc <- get_power(vars, lat = crd_nyc$lat, long = crd_nyc$long) |> 
  mutate(location = "newyorkcity", country = "unitedstates")

power_vancouver <- get_power(vars, lat = crd_vancouver$lat, long = crd_vancouver$long) |> 
  mutate(location = "vancouver", country = "canada")

power_washingtondc <- get_power(vars, lat = crd_washingtondc$lat, long = crd_washingtondc$long) |> 
  mutate(location = "washingtondc", country = "unitedstates")

# Selected locations in Japan
power_hakodate <- get_power(vars, lat = crd_hakodate$lat, long = crd_hakodate$long) |> 
  left_join(crd_hakodate, by = c("LAT" = "lat", "LON" = "long"))

power_kochi <- get_power(vars, lat = crd_kochi$lat, long = crd_kochi$long) |> 
  left_join(crd_kochi, by = c("LAT" = "lat", "LON" = "long"))

power_kumagaya <- get_power(vars, lat = crd_kumagaya$lat, long = crd_kumagaya$long) |> 
  left_join(crd_kumagaya, by = c("LAT" = "lat", "LON" = "long"))

power_mito <- get_power(vars, lat = crd_mito$lat, long = crd_mito$long) |> 
  left_join(crd_mito, by = c("LAT" = "lat", "LON" = "long"))

power_muroran <- get_power(vars, lat = crd_muroran$lat, long = crd_muroran$long) |> 
  left_join(crd_muroran, by = c("LAT" = "lat", "LON" = "long"))
```

### Open Meteo

Use the [`{openmeteo}`](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=openmeteo) package to retrieve weather forecasts from the [Open Meteo API](https://open-meteo.com/).

We have already used the coordinates of the five main locations so all we have to do is to combine them into a list. Because I only want to forecast the five main locations for the current year, I will only load weather forecasts for these locations.

Note that fore locations in Japan and Switzerland, the coordinates for individual trees are given, and I have to select a single location to draw weather forecasts from, hence I choose either the most common location or the one in the middle. Since the coordinates are matched to the nearest weather station, such a choice should not matter much.

```{r}
#| label: list-locations

locations <- list(
  crd_kyoto,
  crd_liestal,
  crd_nyc,
  crd_vancouver,
  crd_washingtondc,
  crd_hakodate,
  crd_kochi,
  crd_kumagaya,
  crd_mito,
  crd_muroran,
  crd_osaka,
  crd_tottori,
  crd_binningen,
  crd_laufenburg,
  crd_albisgutli,
  crd_meteoschweiz,
  crd_witikon
)
```

We create a `get_fcst()` function that calls `openmeteo::weather_forecast()`. We can only get 15 days ahead weather forecasts, and we are about 3 days behind with the NASA POWER data.

```{r}
#| label: get_fcst

get_fcst <- function(loc_gc) {
  
  fcst <- weather_forecast(
    location = c(loc_gc$lat, loc_gc$long), 
    start = as.character(today() - days(3)), 
    end = as.character(today() + days(12)), 
    hourly = c(
      "temperature_2m", 
      "relative_humidity_2m", 
      "pressure_msl",
      "wind_speed_10m"
    ),
    daily = c(
      "temperature_2m_max",
      "temperature_2m_min",
      "precipitation_sum"
    )
  )
  
  fcst$location <- tolower(loc_gc$location)
  
  return(fcst)
}
```

Use the `get_fcst()` function to load the weather forecasts for the five main locations

```{r}
#| label: load-weather-forecasts
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| eval: false

locations_fcst <- map_dfr(.x = locations, .f = get_fcst) |> 
  rename(
    t2m = hourly_temperature_2m,
    t2m_max = daily_temperature_2m_max,
    t2m_min = daily_temperature_2m_min,
    prcp = daily_precipitation_sum,
    rh2m = hourly_relative_humidity_2m,
    ps = hourly_pressure_msl,
    ws10m = hourly_wind_speed_10m
  ) |> 
  group_by(location, date) |> 
  summarise(across(where(is.numeric), ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE))) |> 
  ungroup() |> 
  relocate(location, date, t2m, t2m_max, t2m_min) |> 
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2)))

write_csv(locations_fcst, file = "data/locations_fcst.csv")
```

## Feature engineering

There are multiple methods to calculate features that may be predictive for phenological changes. Most models require hourly recording of temperatures. The **only** feature that *does not depend on hourly temperature records* is the simplest **growing degree days (GDD)** model

$$
\mathrm{GDD} = \max \Biggl\{\frac{\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{max}}+\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{min}}}{2}-\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{base}}, 0\Biggr\}
$$

GDDs are typically **measured from the winter low**. Any temperature below the base temperature is set to the base temperature before calculating the average. Likewise, the maximum temperature is usually capped at 30 °C because most plants and insects do not grow any faster above that temperature.

To calculate more complicated phenological features, we need to interpolate hourly temperatures from the average daily maximum and minimum temperatures.

Compare this to a simple sinusiodal model for the diurnal temperature variation that does not take into account the latitude, or changing patterns over the seasons. The phase shift is the number of hours after midnight when the average daily minimum temperature occurs.

During winter, the maximum temperature occurs between 1pm and 2 pm, during summer, it occurs between 4pm and 5pm.

We calculate GDD contributions for each hour.
Standard GDD with different base temperatures.

Base 4°C is common for cherry blossoms.
We divide by 24 to get daily equivalents.
Alternative base temperatures to try are 0°C and 5°C

GDD with upper threshold (some research suggests 25-30°C as upper threshold)

Modified GDD using optimal growth curve
Triangle function with optimal temperature at 15°C

Beta function approximation for growth response
More complex, smoother curve based on physiological models

Exponential GDD (emphasizes higher temperatures)

GDD with photoperiod modulation (if you have day length data)
This would be a more complex implementation requiring photoperiod data
    
Actual evapotranspiration based GDD
This would account for both temperature and moisture stress

The classic approach in calculating GDD ([Piña, R. A. et al., 2021](https://www.mdpi.com/2223-7747/10/3/502)). If the base temperature is exceeded then the difference in degrees Celsius will be taken into account to calculate the accumulated GDD.

The triangular model following ([Piña, R. A. et al., 2021](https://www.mdpi.com/2223-7747/10/3/502)) takes into account the minimum, maximum and an optimal temperature.

$$
\begin{equation}
  GDD_{1(x_t)} = \begin{cases}
  0\ if\ x_t < t_b \\x_t -t_b\ if\ x_t \geq t_b
  \end{cases}
\end{equation}
$$

 
$$
\begin{equation}
  GDD_{2(x_t)} = \begin{cases}0\ if\ x_t < t_{min} \\\frac{x_t -T_{min}}{T_{opt} - T_{min}}\ if\ T_{min} \leq x_t \leq T_{opt} \\ \frac{x_t -T_{max}}{T_{opt} - T_{max}} if\ T_{opt} \leq x_t \leq T_{max} \\ 0\ if\ x_t \geq T_{max} \end{cases}
\end{equation}
$$

$$
\begin{equation}
  GDD_{3(x_t)} = \begin{cases}
  0\ if\ \left [ \frac{T_{max} - T_{min}}{2} \right ] - t_b < t_b \\
  \left [ \frac{T_{max} - T_{min}}{2} \right ] - t_b\ if\ \left [ \frac{T_{max} - T_{min}}{2} \right ] - t_b > t_b
  \end{cases}
\end{equation}
$$

With the previous equations, the $GDD_{(x_t)}$ are obtained for each day that is between the initial date $t_0$ and one day before flowering $t_{\gamma-1}$, then they are added for each coordinate and the accumulated growth degree days (`AGDD1`, `AGDD2` and `AGDD3`) are obtained.

$$AGDD_i = \sum_{t_0}^{t_{\gamma-1}} GDD_i$$

Calculate chilling degree hour (CDH) with a base temperature of 7 and a lower temperature threshold of zero degrees. Below the lower threshold it is too cold for effective chilling, and above the threshold it is too warm.

Utah chilling units assign different weights to temperature ranges
Ineffective range below 1.4
Low efficiency above 1.4
Optimal chilling between 2.4 and 9.1
Low efficiency between 9.1 and 12.4
Ineffective between 12.4 and 15.9
Negation of chilling between 15.9 and 18
Strong negation above 18

dynamic weights
Too cold below -1
A dynamic weight from a sigmoid function for temperatures between -1 and 13
No weight above 13

Instead of starting from the winter low, we can aggregate **from January 1st** of each year.

**Chilling requirements** of plants are the minimum period of cold weather after which a fruit-bearing tree will blossom productively. They are often expressed in **chill hours**, which can be calculated in different ways, all of which essentially involve adding up the total amount of time in a winter spent at certain temperatures.

Some bulbs have chilling requirements to bloom, and some seeds have chilling requirements to sprout. Biologically, the chilling requirement is a way of ensuring that vernalization occurs.

Chilling temperatures extend **from freezing point** to, depending on the model, 7 °C or even 16 °C. Stone fruit trees and certain other plants of temperate climate develop next year's buds in the summer. In the **autumn** the buds become **dormant**, and the switch to proper, healthy dormancy is triggered by a certain minimum exposure to chilling temperatures. Lack of such exposure results in delayed and substandard foliation, flowering and fruiting. **One chilling unit**, in the simplest models, is equal to **one hour's exposure to the chilling temperature**. These units are **summed up for a whole season**. Advanced models assign different weights to different temperature bands.

Contrary to popular belief, lack of chilling hours does not usually kill a plant, nor prevent a dormant plant from eventually leafing out. However, it may add stress that can be one factor in a plant’s demise; as such, a previously injured plant may not survive long after a warm winter. Fruit trees that do not meet chilling requirements in a given season will not leaf or flower at normal times or for normal durations, and may only produce a few or no fruit.

The simplest model assigns one chilling unit for every full hour at temperatures below 7 °C.

A slightly more sophisticated model excludes freezing temperatures, which do not contribute to proper dormancy cycle, and counts only hours with temperatures between 0 °C and 7 °C.

The **Utah model** assigns different weight to different temperature bands. A full unit per hour is assigned only to temperatures between 3 °C and 9 °C. Maximum effect is achieved at 7 °C. Temperatures between 13 °C and 16 °C, the threshold between chilling and warm weather) have zero weight, and higher temperature have negative weights, as they reduce the beneficial effects of an already accumulated chilling hours.

The model is based on chill-units, where 1 chill-unit is when the tree is exposure between 2.4°C and 9.1°C, being the optimum temperature 6°C . When the temperature is between 9.1°C and 12.4°C,
the chill-unit is 0.5. The chill-units accumulation is 0 when occurs temperature below 1.4 and between 12.5°C and 15.9°C. When the temperature is between 16°C and 18°C, the chill-unit is -0.5. When the temperature is above 18°C, the chill-unit is -1.

Sweet Cherry Model
Quantifies the chill accumulation by means of converting temperatures to chill-units.
The model is based on chill-units, where 1 chill-unit is when the tree is exposure between -2.1°C and 7°C. When the temperature is above 18°C the chill-unit is -1. The chill-units accumulation is 0 when occurs temperature between 14°C and 16°C
This model was make for quantifying the chill accumulation rates to ’Sweetheart’ Sweet Cherry.
We aren’t recommended the application for others species.
GUAK, Sunghee & NEILSEN, Denise. (2013). Chill Unit Models for Predicting Dormancy Completion of Floral Buds in Apple and Sweet Cherry.

Dynamic Model
Quantifies the chill accumulation with dynamic equation (two-steps).
The model is based on dynamic accumulation, by means of the relationship between temperatures.
The dynamic model assumes that the accumulated chill-units are not annulled by high temperatures.
FISHMAN, Svetlana, EREZ, A. & COUVILLON, G. A. (1987). The Temperature Dependence
of Dormancy Breaking in Plants: Computer Simulation of Processes Studied Under Controlled Temperatures. J. Theor. Biol.

GDH Model - Anderson - for heat accumulation

The GDH Model is based on base and optimum temperature. The base temperature is 4°C. The optimum and critical temperature are 25°C and 36°C, respectively.

Anderson, J. L. et al. 1986. Validation of chill unit and flower bud phenology models for "Montmorency" sour cherry. Acta Horticulturae - Modelling in Fruit Research.

GDH Model - Richardson - for heat accumulation

The GDH model is based on the subtraction of the base temperature of each hourly temperature between 4.5°C and 25°C. The temperature of the base is 4.5°C. Therefore, accumulation under temperatures below 4.5°C and above 25°C is zero.

RICHARDSON, E.A. et al. 1975. Pheno-climatography of spring 249 peach bud development. HortScience.

Southwick et al. wrote that neither of these models is accurate enough to account for application of rest-breaking agents widely used in modern farming. They advocated the use of a **dynamic model** tailored to the **two-stage** explanation of dormancy.

- Utah (Richardson et al., 1974, ISSN:0018-5345)

- Positive Chill Units - PCU (Linsley-Noaks et al., 1995, ISSN:1017-0316)

- GDH-A - Growing Degree Hours by Anderson et al.(1986, ISSN:0567-7572)

- GDH-R - Growing Degree Hours by Richardson et al.(1975, ISSN:0018-5345)

- North Carolina (Shaltout e Unrath, 1983, ISSN:0003-1062)

- Landsberg Model (Landsberg, 1974, ISSN:0305-7364)

- Q10 Model (Bidabe, 1967, ISSN:0031-9368)

- Jones Model (Jones et al., 2013 <doi:10.1111/j.1438-8677.2012.00590.x>)

- Low-Chill Model (Gilreath and Buchanan, 1981, ISSN:0003-1062)

- Model for Cherry "Sweetheart" (Guak and Nielsen, 2013 <doi:10.1007/s13580-013-0140-9>), 

- Model for apple "Gala" (Guak and Nielsen, 2013 <doi:10.1007/s13580-013-0140-9>)

- Taiwan Model (Lu et al., 2012 <doi:10.17660/ActaHortic.2012.962.35>)

- Dynamic Model (Fishman et al., 1987, ISSN:0022-5193) adapted from the function Dynamic_Model() of the 'chillR' package (Luedeling, 2018)

- Unified Model (Chuine et al., 2016 <doi:10.1111/gcb.13383>)

- Heat Restriction model

The Sweet Cherry Model uses the function `cherry_model(x, total = TRUE)` from the `{ChillModels}` package.

It quantifies the chill accumulation by means of converting temperatures to chill-units.
The argument `x` is a vector containing temperature values (Celsius-degree). For `total = TRUE`, the total value of accumulation is returned, for  `total = FALSE`, the value of `chillunit` for each temperature is returned (default is `TRUE`).

The model is based on chill-units, where 1 chill-unit is when the tree is exposed to between -2.1°C and 7°C. When the temperature is above 18°C the chill-unit is -1. The chill-units accumulation is 0 when occurs temperature between 14°C and 16°C.

The function returns values the chill-units for each temperature of vector (Total = FALSE), or returns the chill-units accumulation (Total = TRUE).

This model was make for quantifying the chill accumulation rates to ’Sweetheart’ Sweet Cherry. We don’t recommended the application for others species.

First we interpolate hourly temperatures

```{r}
#| label: interpolate-hourly-temperatures

hourly_temp <- power_cherry |>
  group_by(location, year) |>
  mutate(
    hourly_temps = map2(
      .x = t2m_min, 
      .y = t2m_max, 
      .f = function(t2m_min, t2m_max) {
        hours <- 0:23
        amplitude <- (t2m_max - t2m_min) / 2
        midpoint <- (t2m_max + t2m_min) / 2
        phase_shift <- 3
        period <- 24
      
        temps <- midpoint - amplitude * cos(2 * pi * (hours - phase_shift) / period)
      return(temps)
    })
  ) 
```

Then we apply some of the growing degree day formulas to the hourly temperatures

```{r}
#| label: hourly-gdd

hourly_features <- hourly_temp |> 
  unnest(hourly_temps) |> 
  group_by(location, year, date) |> 
  mutate(
    gdh = pmax(0, hourly_temps - 4),
    cdh = case_when(hourly_temps <= 0.00 ~ 0, hourly_temps >= 7.00 ~ 0, TRUE ~ 7.00 - hourly_temps)
  )
```

Aggregate the hourly features to a daily level

```{r}
hourly_features |> 
  group_by(location, date) |> 
  summarise(
    gdh = sum(gdh),
    cdh = sum(cdh)
  ) |> 
  ungroup()
```






### Midrange temperature

We create the midrange temperature, the average of the maximum and the minimum average temperature measured on a specific day.

```{r}
#| label: create-t2m_range

power_cherry <- power_cherry |> 
  mutate(t2m_range = (t2m_max + t2m_min) / 2) |> 
  relocate(location, date, t2m, t2m_max, t2m_min, t2m_range)
```

## Quetelet's law of flowering plants

Quetelet assumed that for a plant to start blooming, the cumulative sum of the squared daily temperature aggregated since the day of the last frost needed to exceed a certain threshold, which depends on the species. 

```{r}
#| label: create-qlaw

power_qlaw <- power_cherry |> 
  mutate(year = year(date), doy = yday(date)) |> 
  group_by(location, year) |> 
  filter(date >= max(date[which(t2m_range < 0) + 1])) |> 
  mutate(qlaw = round(cumsum(t2m_range)^2), 2) |> 
  ungroup() |> 
  select(-c(year, doy))


power_cherry <- power_cherry |> 
  left_join(y = power_qlaw |> select(location, date, qlaw), join_by(location, date))

power_cherry <- power_cherry |> 
  mutate(qlaw = if_else(is.na(qlaw), 0, qlaw))
```

### Aggregated precipitation since January 1st

We use the variable daily measured precipitation (in mm) to calculate accumulated precipitation starting from January 1st of the year of the observation date. 

```{r}
#| label: create-aprcp

power_cherry <- power_cherry |> 
  group_by(location, year) |> 
  arrange(location, year, date) |> 
  mutate(aprcp = cumsum(prcp)) |> 
  ungroup()
```

### Aggregated growing degree days since January 1st

```{r}
colnames(kyoto_hours)[ncol(kyoto_hours)] <- "Temp_empirical"

kyoto_ideal <- kyoto_ideal[, c("Year", "Month", "Day", "Hour", "Temp")]
colnames(kyoto_ideal)[ncol(kyoto_ideal)] <- "Temp_ideal"

station_list_kyoto <- handle_gsod(

)

station_list_kyoto |> 
  filter(chillR_code == "47759099999")


weather_kyoto <- handle_gsod(

  time_interval = c(1970, 2025)

cleaned_weather_kyoto <- handle_gsod(weather_kyoto)
cleaned_weather_kyoto[[1]][1:20, ]

weather_kyoto <- KA_weather |>
  make_all_day_table()

Tmin_int <- interpolate_gaps(weather[,"Tmin"])

weather <- weather %>% mutate(Tmin = Tmin_int$interp,
                              Tmin_interpolated = Tmin_int$missing)
```
