There are multiple ways to use growing degree days.

To simplify the calculation, we use January 1 of each year as the starting date for the calculations.

We need to define a base temperature, $t_{b}$ at which the cherry trees start to "absorb" thermal energy. Temperatures between 3°C and 5°C are commonly chosen.

The daily temperatures have to be derived from the available air temperatures `t2m`, `t2m_max`, `t2m_min` and `t2m_range`.

Software exists that will optimize the temperature threshold, but 

I choose the *basal temperature* or limit $(t_b)$ to consider thermal absorption as 5°C, however, the function in question has an argument named `t_base` that allows testing with different values. The daily temperatures $x_t$ (variables `TS`, `TS_MAX`, `TS_MIN`) are used for this calculation. Due to time issues I was not able to experiment enough to estimate optimal values of $t_b$ and $t_0$. The three ways of calculating GDD are described below ([Piña, R. A. et al., 2021](https://www.mdpi.com/2223-7747/10/3/502); [McCaster, G. S. & Wilhelm , W.W., 1997](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0168192397000270#:~:text=The%20basic%20equation%20used%20is,BASE%20is%20the%20base%20temperature .)):
     - **Equation 1:** classic approach in calculating GDD ([Piña, R. A. et al., 2021](https://www.mdpi.com/2223-7747/10/3/502)). If a basal temperature $t_b = 5$ is exceeded then the difference in degrees Celsius will be taken into account to calculate the accumulated GDD (`AGDD1`).
     - **Equation 2:** Equation 2 ([Piña, R. A. et al., 2021](https://www.mdpi.com/2223-7747/10/3/502)) represents the *triangular model of GDD*, this model represents a non-linear triangular function based on temperatures. This equation takes into account the minimum, maximum temperature and an *optimal temperature*. Since I do not have enough information to consider an optimal temperature, I use the same basal temperature with a value of 5°C.
     - **Equation 3:** this equation is another classic approximation ([McCaster, G. S. & Wilhelm, W.W., 1997](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0168192397000270#:~: text=The%20basic%20equation%20used%20is,BASE%20is%20the%20base%20temperature.)) for the calculation of GDD, where the maximum and minimum temperature is used. In this case *equation 1* coincides with this, however, for the first I use the average temperature directly, in *equation 2* I use the average of the maximum and minimum temperatures. I verified that the results are not the same from the three methods.

$$
\begin{equation}
  GDD_{1(x_t)} = \begin{cases}
  0\ if\ x_t < t_b \\x_t -t_b\ if\ x_t \geq t_b
  \end{cases}
\end{equation}
$$

 
$$
\begin{equation}
  GDD_{2(x_t)} = \begin{cases}0\ if\ x_t < t_{min} \\\frac{x_t -T_{min}}{T_{opt} - T_{min}}\ if\ T_{min} \leq x_t \leq T_{opt} \\ \frac{x_t -T_{max}}{T_{opt} - T_{max}} if\ T_{opt} \leq x_t \leq T_{max} \\ 0\ if\ x_t \geq T_{max} \end{cases}
\end{equation}
$$

$$
\begin{equation}
  GDD_{3(x_t)} = \begin{cases}
  0\ if\ \left [ \frac{T_{max} - T_{min}}{2} \right ] - t_b < t_b \\
  \left [ \frac{T_{max} - T_{min}}{2} \right ] - t_b\ if\ \left [ \frac{T_{max} - T_{min}}{2} \right ] - t_b > t_b
  \end{cases}
\end{equation}
$$

With the previous equations, the $GDD_{(x_t)}$ are obtained for each day that is between the initial date $t_0$ and one day before flowering $t_{\gamma-1}$, then they are added for each coordinate and the accumulated growth degree days (`AGDD1`, `AGDD2` and `AGDD3`) are obtained.

$$AGDD_i = \sum_{t_0}^{t_{\gamma-1}} GDD_i$$

Growing Degree Day calculations.

First calculate hourly temperatures by interpolating daily average minimum and maximum temperatures with a sinusoidal model for diurnal temperature curve.

For each day, create 24 hourly estimates.

Consider the phase shift, the number of hours after midnight when minimum occurs


```{r}
power_cherry |> 
  group_by(location, year) |> 
  mutate(
    hourly_temps = map2(temp_min, temp_max, function(tmin, tmax) {
  
      hours <- 0:23
      amplitude <- (tmax - tmin) / 2
      midpoint <- (tmax + tmin) / 2
      phase_shift <- 4
      period <- 24
      
      temps <- midpoint + amplitude * sin(2 * pi * (hours - phase_shift) / period)
      return(temps)
    })
  ) %>%
  # Unnest to get hourly data
  unnest(hourly_temps) %>%
  group_by(location_id, year, date, hour = rep(0:23, n() / 24)) %>%
  # Calculate GDD contributions for each hour
  mutate(
    # Standard GDD with different base temperatures
    # Base 4°C is common for cherry blossoms
    gdd_base4 = pmax(0, hourly_temps - 4) / 24,  # Divide by 24 to get daily equivalent
    
    # Alternative base temperatures to try
    gdd_base0 = pmax(0, hourly_temps - 0) / 24,
    gdd_base5 = pmax(0, hourly_temps - 5) / 24,
    
    # GDD with upper threshold (some research suggests 25-30°C as upper threshold)
    gdd_base4_cap25 = case_when(
      hourly_temps < 4 ~ 0,
      hourly_temps > 25 ~ (25 - 4) / 24,
      TRUE ~ (hourly_temps - 4) / 24
    ),
    
    # Modified GDD using optimal growth curve
    # Triangle function with optimal temperature at 15°C
    triangle_gdd = case_when(
      hourly_temps <= 4 ~ 0,
      hourly_temps > 4 & hourly_temps <= 15 ~ 
        (hourly_temps - 4) * (1 / (15 - 4)) / 24,
      hourly_temps > 15 & hourly_temps <= 25 ~ 
        (25 - hourly_temps) * (1 / (25 - 15)) / 24,
      TRUE ~ 0
    ),
    
    # Beta function approximation for growth response
    # More complex, smoother curve based on physiological models
    beta_gdd = case_when(
      hourly_temps <= 0 ~ 0,
      hourly_temps >= 30 ~ 0,
      TRUE ~ (((hourly_temps - 0) / (16 - 0))^1.5) * 
             (1 - ((hourly_temps - 0) / (30 - 0))^2.5) / 24
    ),
    
    # Exponential GDD (emphasizes higher temperatures)
    exp_gdd = ifelse(hourly_temps > 4, 
                    (1.05^(hourly_temps - 4) - 1) / 24, 
                    0),
    
    # GDD with photoperiod modulation (if you have day length data)
    # This would be a more complex implementation requiring photoperiod data
    
    # Actual evapotranspiration based GDD (simplified)
    # This would account for both temperature and moisture stress
    aet_gdd = case_when(
      hourly_temps <= 4 ~ 0,
      TRUE ~ (hourly_temps - 4) / 24 # This would be multiplied by a moisture factor
    )
  )

# Aggregate by day
gdd_daily <- weather_features %>%
  group_by(location_id, year, date) %>%
  summarize(
    # Sum hourly contributions to get daily values
    daily_gdd_base4 = sum(gdd_base4),
    daily_gdd_base0 = sum(gdd_base0),
    daily_gdd_base5 = sum(gdd_base5),
    daily_gdd_base4_cap25 = sum(gdd_base4_cap25),
    daily_triangle_gdd = sum(triangle_gdd),
    daily_beta_gdd = sum(beta_gdd),
    daily_exp_gdd = sum(exp_gdd),
    daily_aet_gdd = sum(aet_gdd),
    
    # Daily mean temperature (for reference)
    daily_mean_temp = mean(hourly_temps),
    
    # Day-night temperature difference (can affect development)
    temp_range = max(hourly_temps) - min(hourly_temps),
    
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  # Calculate cumulative values
  group_by(location_id, year) %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(
    # Standard cumulative GDD
    cum_gdd_base4 = cumsum(daily_gdd_base4),
    cum_gdd_base0 = cumsum(daily_gdd_base0),
    cum_gdd_base5 = cumsum(daily_gdd_base5),
    cum_gdd_base4_cap25 = cumsum(daily_gdd_base4_cap25),
    cum_triangle_gdd = cumsum(daily_triangle_gdd),
    cum_beta_gdd = cumsum(daily_beta_gdd),
    cum_exp_gdd = cumsum(daily_exp_gdd),
    cum_aet_gdd = cumsum(daily_aet_gdd),
    
    # Rate of GDD accumulation (1-week moving average)
    gdd_rate = slider::slide_dbl(daily_gdd_base4, mean, .before = 6, .complete = TRUE),
    
    # Create seasonal restart of GDD (e.g., after Jan 1)
    # For areas where winter GDD might not be relevant
    doy = yday(date),
    seasonal_start = doy == 1,
    season_group = cumsum(seasonal_start),
    
    # Calculate GDD since seasonal start
    season_gdd = cumsum(ifelse(!is.na(season_group) & season_group == season_group[1], 
                               daily_gdd_base4, 0))
  )
```


```{r}
# Extract monthly GDD summaries
monthly_gdd <- gdd_daily %>%
  mutate(month = month(date)) %>%
  group_by(location_id, year, month) %>%
  summarize(
    # Monthly totals
    monthly_gdd_base4 = sum(daily_gdd_base4, na.rm = TRUE),
    monthly_gdd_base0 = sum(daily_gdd_base0, na.rm = TRUE),
    monthly_gdd_base5 = sum(daily_gdd_base5, na.rm = TRUE),
    monthly_gdd_base4_cap25 = sum(daily_gdd_base4_cap25, na.rm = TRUE),
    monthly_triangle_gdd = sum(daily_triangle_gdd, na.rm = TRUE),
    monthly_beta_gdd = sum(daily_beta_gdd, na.rm = TRUE),
    monthly_exp_gdd = sum(daily_exp_gdd, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    # End of month cumulative values
    end_of_month_cum_gdd_base4 = last(cum_gdd_base4),
    end_of_month_cum_triangle_gdd = last(cum_triangle_gdd),
    end_of_month_cum_beta_gdd = last(cum_beta_gdd),
    
    # Average daily GDD rate for the month
    avg_gdd_rate = mean(gdd_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    # Temperature extremes
    max_temp = max(daily_mean_temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_temp = min(daily_mean_temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    # Day-night variation average
    avg_temp_range = mean(temp_range, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  # Convert to wide format for model features
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = c(location_id, year),
    names_from = month,
    values_from = c(monthly_gdd_base4, monthly_gdd_base0, monthly_gdd_base5, 
                   monthly_gdd_base4_cap25, monthly_triangle_gdd, monthly_beta_gdd,
                   monthly_exp_gdd, end_of_month_cum_gdd_base4, 
                   end_of_month_cum_triangle_gdd, end_of_month_cum_beta_gdd,
                   avg_gdd_rate, max_temp, min_temp, avg_temp_range),
    names_prefix = "month"
  )

# Join with your model data
model_data_enhanced <- model_data %>%
  left_join(monthly_gdd, by = c("location_id", "year"))
```


We create the accumulated growing degree days (AGDD) as the sum of growing degree days (GDD) since January 1st, where GDD are calculated as the number of degrees C by which each day's midrange temperature exceeds a base temperature, which can be 0 degrees C, or a species-specific base temperature, such as 4.3 degrees C for Yoshino cherry trees. If the midrange temperature does not exceed the base temperature on a given day, no growing degree days are counted. See more at <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Growing_degree-day>.

```{r}
#| label: create-agdd

base_temp <- 4.0

power_cherry <- power_cherry |> 
  group_by(location, year) |> 
  arrange(location, year, date) |> 
  mutate(agdd = cumsum(pmax(t2m_range - base_temp, 0))) |> 
  ungroup()
```


### Aggregated Chilling hours (temperatures between 0-7°C) since October 1st

Key Differences Between Chilling Methods

Chilling Hours (CH): Simple count of hours below a threshold (typically 7°C)

Easiest to calculate but least physiologically accurate


Chilling Degree Hours (CDH): Accumulation of degrees below the threshold

Example: 3°C for one hour = 4 CDH (7°C - 3°C = 4 degrees × 1 hour)
More accurate as it accounts for temperature intensity


Utah Model: Assigns weights to different temperature ranges

Recognizes that chilling isn't simply linear with temperature
Accounts for negation of chilling by warm temperatures


Dynamic Model: Most physiologically accurate

Models a two-step process in the plant
Better performs across diverse climates

```{r}
# Calculate chilling degree hours (CDH)
weather_features <- weather %>%
  group_by(location_id, year = year(date)) %>%
  mutate(
    # First calculate hourly temperatures using a simple interpolation
    # For each day, create 24 hourly estimates
    hourly_temps = map2(temp_min, temp_max, function(tmin, tmax) {
      # Simple sinusoidal model for diurnal temperature curve
      # Minimum temperature typically occurs around 4am, maximum around 2pm
      hours <- 0:23
      amplitude <- (tmax - tmin) / 2
      midpoint <- (tmax + tmin) / 2
      phase_shift <- 4  # Hours after midnight when minimum occurs
      period <- 24      # Hours
      
      temps <- midpoint + amplitude * sin(2 * pi * (hours - phase_shift) / period)
      return(temps)
    })
  ) %>%
  # Unnest to get hourly data
  unnest(hourly_temps) %>%
  group_by(location_id, year, date, hour = rep(0:23, n() / 24)) %>%
  # Calculate chilling contribution for each hour
  mutate(
    # Define temperature thresholds for chilling
    base_temp = 7.0,    # Upper threshold for chilling (°C)
    lower_temp = 0.0,   # Lower threshold for chilling (°C)
    
    # Calculate chilling degree hour (CDH)
    cdh = case_when(
      hourly_temps <= lower_temp ~ 0,  # Too cold for effective chilling
      hourly_temps >= base_temp ~ 0,   # Too warm for chilling
      TRUE ~ base_temp - hourly_temps  # Chilling degrees proportional to temperature below base
    ),
    
    # Utah model weights (optional enhancement - different temperature ranges have different effectiveness)
    utah_weight = case_when(
      hourly_temps < 1.4 ~ 0,                  # Ineffective range
      hourly_temps >= 1.4 & hourly_temps < 2.4 ~ 0.5,  # Low efficiency
      hourly_temps >= 2.4 & hourly_temps < 9.1 ~ 1.0,  # Optimal chilling
      hourly_temps >= 9.1 & hourly_temps < 12.4 ~ 0.5, # Low efficiency 
      hourly_temps >= 12.4 & hourly_temps < 15.9 ~ 0,  # Ineffective
      hourly_temps >= 15.9 & hourly_temps < 18.0 ~ -0.5, # Negation of chilling
      hourly_temps >= 18.0 ~ -1.0                       # Strong negation
    ),
    
    # Utah model chilling units
    utah_cu = utah_weight,
    
    # Dynamic Model chilling portions (simplified approximation)
    # The actual Dynamic Model is more complex with an intermediate state
    dynamic_weight = case_when(
      hourly_temps < -1.0 ~ 0,                 # Too cold
      hourly_temps >= -1.0 & hourly_temps < 13.0 ~ 
        (exp(3.1 * (hourly_temps - (-1.0)) / (13.0 - (-1.0))) - 
           exp(-3.1 * (hourly_temps - (-1.0)) / (13.0 - (-1.0)))) / 
        (exp(3.1) - exp(-3.1)), # Approximately sigmoid
      TRUE ~ 0                                  # Too warm
    )
  )

# Aggregate by day and calculate cumulative values
chilling_daily <- weather_features %>%
  group_by(location_id, year, date) %>%
  summarize(
    daily_cdh = sum(cdh),
    daily_utah = sum(utah_cu),
    daily_dynamic = sum(dynamic_weight) / 24,  # Convert to portions (approx)
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  group_by(location_id, year) %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(
    cum_cdh = cumsum(daily_cdh),
    cum_utah = cumsum(daily_utah),
    cum_dynamic = cumsum(daily_dynamic)
  )

# Extract monthly chilling summaries
monthly_chilling <- chilling_daily %>%
  mutate(month = month(date)) %>%
  group_by(location_id, year, month) %>%
  summarize(
    monthly_cdh = sum(daily_cdh),
    monthly_utah = sum(daily_utah),
    monthly_dynamic = sum(daily_dynamic),
    end_of_month_cum_cdh = last(cum_cdh),
    end_of_month_cum_utah = last(cum_utah),
    end_of_month_cum_dynamic = last(cum_dynamic),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  # Convert to wide format for model features
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = c(location_id, year),
    names_from = month,
    values_from = c(monthly_cdh, monthly_utah, monthly_dynamic, 
                   end_of_month_cum_cdh, end_of_month_cum_utah, end_of_month_cum_dynamic),
    names_prefix = "month"
  )

# Join with your existing model data
model_data_enhanced <- model_data %>%
  left_join(monthly_chilling, by = c("location_id", "year"))
```


We can calculate chilling hours (CDD) and accumulated chilling degree days (ACDD) since October 1st. We count CDDs whenever the midrange temperature is below a threshold of 7 degrees Celsius, and we accumulate until December 31st of each year. If the midrange temperature stays above the threshold, no GDDs are counted. See more at <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chilling_requirement>.

```{r}
#| label: create-achill

power_achill <- power_cherry |> 
  filter(date >= paste0(year, "-09-01")) |> 
  mutate(
    chill = ifelse(t2m_min >= 0 & t2m_max <= 7, 24, 
                   ifelse(t2m_min < 0 & t2m_max > 7, 0,
                   ifelse(t2m_min < 0, (t2m_max - 0)/(t2m_max - t2m_min) * 24,
                   (7 - t2m_min)/(t2m_max - t2m_min) * 24)))
  ) |>
  group_by(location, year) |> 
  arrange(location, year, date) |> 
  mutate(achill = cumsum(chill)) |> 
  ungroup()

power_cherry <- power_cherry |> 
  left_join(y = power_acdd |> select(location, date, acdd), join_by(location, date))

power_cherry <- power_cherry |> 
  mutate(acdd = if_else(is.na(acdd), 0, acdd))
```

## Select time range

I select only days between October 1st and the last available forecast date of the current year. That way, the model won't rely on data which is not available on the day of the submission deadline.

```{r}
#| label: select-time-range

last_fcst_date <- power_cherry |> 
  select(date) |>
  pull() |> 
  max()

power_cherry <- power_cherry |> 
  mutate(day = yday(date)) |> 
  relocate(location, date, day) |> 
  # filter(day %in% c(1:yday(last_fcst_date)))
  filter(day %in% c(yday(date("1980-09-01")):366, 1:yday(last_fcst_date)))
```

## Temporal aggregation

We need to decide at which temporal granularity we want our predictors.

### Seasons

```{r}
#| label: aggregate-to-seasons

df_seasons <- power_cherry |> 
  mutate(year = year(date), month = month(date)) |> 
  mutate(
    season = case_when(
      month %in% c(12, 1, 2) ~ "winter",
      month %in% c(3, 4, 5) ~ "spring",
      month %in% c(6, 7, 8) ~ "summer",
      month %in% c(9, 10, 11) ~ "winter"
    )
  ) |> 
  mutate(year = if_else(month == 12, year + 1, year)) |> 
  group_by(location, year, season) |> 
  summarise(across(where(is.numeric), mean), .groups = "drop") |> 
  ungroup() |> 
  pivot_longer(cols = -c(location, year, season), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") |> 
  mutate(variable = paste0(variable, "_", season)) |> 
  select(-season) |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = value)

cherry_seasons <- cherry |> 
  inner_join(y = df_seasons, join_by(year, location)) |> 
  select(-c(lat, long, alt, bloom_date))
```

### Months

```{r}
#| label: aggregate-to-months

df_months <- power_cherry |> 
  mutate(year = year(date), month = month(date, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE)) |> 
  group_by(location, year, month) |> 
  summarise(across(where(is.numeric), mean), .groups = "drop") |> 
  ungroup() |> 
  pivot_longer(cols = -c(location, year, month), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") |> 
  mutate(variable = paste0(variable, "_", month)) |> 
  select(-c(month)) |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = value)

cherry_months <- cherry |> 
  inner_join(y = df_months, join_by(year, location)) |> 
  select(-c(lat, long, alt, bloom_date))
```

### Weeks

```{r}
#| label: aggregate-to-weeks

df_weeks <- power_cherry |> 
  mutate(year = year(date), week = week(date)) |> 
  select(-date) |> 
  group_by(location, year, week) |> 
  summarise(across(where(is.numeric), mean), .groups = "drop") |> 
  ungroup() |> 
  pivot_longer(cols = -c(location, year, week), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") |> 
  mutate(variable = paste0(variable, "_w_", week)) |> 
  select(-week) |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = value)

cherry_weeks <- cherry |> 
  inner_join(y = df_weeks, join_by(year, location)) |> 
  select(-c(lat, long, alt, bloom_date))
```

### Days

```{r}
#| label: aggregate-to-days
#| warning: true

df_days <- power_cherry |> 
  mutate(year = year(date), day = yday(date)) |> 
  relocate(location, year, day, date) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -c(location, year, day, date), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") |> 
  mutate(variable = paste0(variable, "_d_", day)) |> 
  select(-c(day, date)) |> 
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c(location, year), names_from = variable, values_from = value)

cherry_days <- cherry |> 
  inner_join(y = df_days, join_by(year, location)) |> 
  select(-c(lat, long, alt, bloom_date))
```

## Exploratory data analysis (EDA)

### Linear model

A simple linear model can help us understand how predictive a feature is

Plot the average maximum temperature in winter `t2m_max_winter`

```{r}
#| label: fig-t2m_max_winter
#| fig-cap: "Average maximum winter temperature (Dec. 1st of the previous year until end of February)"

cherry_seasons |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = t2m_max_winter)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Average maximum winter temperature (°C)") +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(location)) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(1970, 2025)) +
  theme_light()
```

We fit a linear model with different intercepts and time trends for each location and a weather effect. We can add interaction effects to the temperature data too if we want.

```{r}
#| label: fit-lin-t2m_max_winter

lm_mod <- linear_reg(mode = "regression", engine = "lm")

lm_fit <- lm_mod |> 
  fit(
    formula = bloom_doy ~ 0 + location + location:year + location:t2m_max_winter, 
    data = cherry_seasons
  )
```

Create fitted values for the bast observations

```{r}
#| label: predictions-t2m_max_winter

mean_pred <- predict(object = lm_fit, new_data = cherry_seasons)
```

Let's plot the predictions and the actual data

```{r}
#| label: fig-predictions-t2m_max_winter
#| fig-cap: "Predictions from linear time trend and average maximum winter temperature"

cherry_seasons |> 
  bind_cols(mean_pred) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = bloom_doy)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = .pred)) +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(location)) +
  theme_light()
```

Because `t2m_max_winter` shows a clear upwards trend over the past twenty years, we are able model the trend towards earlier peak bloom dates quite well.

We see that the model with the linear time trend and the predictor `t2m_max_winter` does predict the data better than with only the linear time trend. We can assume that a model with `t2m_max_spring` would explain the data even better, but unfortunately, we don't have data for the spring of this year.

We also see that the average temperature in Kyoto is too mild to explain much of the variance in peak bloom times.

Plot a linear time trend

```{r}
cherry_seasons |>
```


### Decision tree

Fit a decision tree for exploratory data analysis. We use the `{parsnip}` package to create a model that runs on the `"rpart"` engine, and we use the `rpart.plot` package to plot the decision tree.

```{r}
set.seed(456)

# Create a {parsnip} model that runs on the "rpart" engine
cart_specs <- decision_tree(
  tree_depth = 10,
  cost_complexity = 0.001
  ) |>
  set_mode("regression") |>
  set_engine("rpart")

# fit the model 
cart_fit <- cart_specs |>
  fit(
    formula = bloom_doy ~ ., 
    data = cherry_days
  )

# Visualize with {rpart.plot}
cart_fit$fit |> 
  rpart.plot()
```

On a seasonal aggregation level, aggregated growing degree days (AGDD) are the most important predictor.

### Variable importance plot (VIP)

Use the `{vip}` package to create a variable importance plot (VIP)

```{r}
cart_fit |> 
  vip()
```

## Modeling

We can combine the seasonal, monthly, weekly and daily predictors if we want to.

```{r}
cherry_full <- bind_cols(
  cherry_seasons,
  cherry_months |> select(-c(location, year, bloom_doy))
  # cherry_weeks |> select(-c(location, year, bloom_doy)),
  # cherry_days |> select(-c(location, year, bloom_doy))
)

cherry_full
```


### Data spending

We need to split these observations randomly into
- a training set that will be used to train the model
- a test set that will be used to compare the performance different models against each other

Because the number of observations are so small, any random split will have huge consequences. Stratified splitting may somewhat help here.

We use the `{rsample}` function `initial_split()` or `initial_time_split()` to create a test set and a training set. The first let's you use the argument `strata = bloom_doy`, the latter will consider the time when splitting the data.

```{r}
#| label: initial-split
#| eval: true

set.seed(123)

cherry_data <- cherry_days

data_split <- initial_split(
  data = cherry_data |> 
    filter(year < year(Sys.Date())), 
  prop = 2/3, 
  strata = bloom_doy
)

data_train <- training(data_split)
data_test  <- testing(data_split)
```

### Pre-processing

We define a recipe for the pre-processing using the `{recipes}` package

```{r}
#| label: preprocessing
#| eval: true

cherry_recipe <- recipe(formula = bloom_doy ~ ., data = data_train) |>
  step_zv(all_nominal_predictors()) |> 
  step_novel(all_nominal_predictors()) |> 
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |> 
  step_harmonic(year, frequency = 1 / 11, cycle_size = 1) |> 
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())
```

### Tuning

Within the training stage we will evaluate hyperparameters via cross-validation.
In 10-fold cross validation (CV), we will randomly split the training set into 10 roughly equally-sized subsets, and we will repeatedly fit the model on 9 of these folds, which constitute the *analysis* set, and evaluate the models' performance on the remaining fold, the *assessment* set.

We also want to ensure the sampling is stratified. This ensures the samples represent all quantiles of bloom_doy. We use the option `strata = bloom_doy` in `vfold_cv()`.

```{r}
set.seed(123)

folds <- vfold_cv(data_train, v = 10, strata = bloom_doy)
```

- Penalized regression: <https://parsnip.tidymodels.org//reference/details_linear_reg_glmnet.html>

- Random forest with ranger: <https://parsnip.tidymodels.org//reference/details_rand_forest_ranger.html>

- XGBoost: <https://parsnip.tidymodels.org/reference/details_boost_tree_xgboost.html>

- LightGBM: <https://parsnip.tidymodels.org/reference/details_boost_tree_lightgbm.html>

```{r}
linear_mod <- linear_reg() |> 
  set_mode("regression") |> 
  set_engine("lm")

pca_tune_mod <- linear_reg() |> 
  set_mode("regression") |> 
  set_engine("lm")

ridge_tune_mod <- linear_reg(
  mixture = 0, 
  penalty = tune()
  ) |> 
  set_mode("regression") |> 
  set_engine("glmnet")

lasso_tune_mod <- linear_reg(
  mixture = 1, 
  penalty = tune()
  ) |> 
  set_mode("regression") |> 
  set_engine("glmnet")

rf_tune_mod <- rand_forest(
  trees = tune(),
  mtry = tune(),
  min_n = tune()
  ) |> 
  set_engine("ranger", num.threads = 6, importance = "impurity") |> 
  set_mode("regression")

xgb_tune_mod <- boost_tree(
  mtry = tune(),
  trees = tune(),
  tree_depth = tune(),
  learn_rate = tune(),
  loss_reduction = tune()
  ) |>
  set_engine("xgboost", num.threads = 6) |> 
  set_mode("regression")

lgb_tune_mod <- boost_tree(
  mtry = tune(),
  trees = tune(),
  tree_depth = tune(),
  learn_rate = tune(),
  loss_reduction = tune()
  ) |> 
  set_engine("lightgbm", num.threads = 6) |> 
  set_mode("regression")

cub_tune_mod <- cubist_rules(
  committees = tune(),
  neighbors = tune(),
  max_rules = tune()
  ) |>
  set_engine("Cubist") |>
  set_mode("regression")
```


```{r}
pca_grid <- grid_random(
  threshold(range = c(0, 1)), 
  size = 50
)

ridge_grid <- grid_random(
  penalty(range = c(-10, 10)),
  size = 50
)

lasso_grid <- grid_random(
  penalty(range = c(-10, 10)),
  size = 50
)

rf_grid <- grid_random(
  trees(range = c(100, 500)),
  mtry(range = c(1, 30)),
  min_n(range = c(1, 10)),
  size = 20
)

xgb_grid <- grid_random(
  trees(range = c(100, 500)),
  tree_depth(range = c(1, 10)),
  learn_rate(range = c(0.1, 0.005)),
  mtry(range = c(1, 30)),
  loss_reduction(range = c(0, 0.1)),
  size = 20
)

lgb_grid <- grid_random(
  trees(range = c(100, 500)),
  tree_depth(range = c(1, 10)),
  learn_rate(range = c(0.1, 0.005)),
  mtry(range = c(1, 30)),
  loss_reduction(range = c(0, 0.1)),
  size = 30
)

cub_grid <- grid_random(
  committees(range = c(30, 45)),
  neighbors(range = c(1, 10)),
  max_rules(range = c(5, 30)),
  size = 30
)
```

Tune the models using the k-fold CV on the grid that we have just created using the `{tune}` function `tune_grid()`. Define the metrics with the `{yardstick}` function `metric_set()`, specifying `mae()` and `mae()`.

To speed up the tuning process, we use the `tune_race_anova()` function from the `{finetune}` package to speed up the tuning process.

```{r}
pca_tune_res <- tune_grid(
  object = workflow() |> 
    add_recipe(cherry_recipe) |> 
    step_pca(all_predictors(), threshold = tune()) |> 
    add_model(pca_tune_mod),
  resamples = folds, 
  grid = pca_grid
)

ridge_tune_res <- tune_grid(
  object = workflow() |> 
    add_recipe(cherry_recipe) |> 
    add_model(ridge_tune_mod),
  resamples = folds, 
  grid = ridge_grid
)

lasso_tune_res <- tune_grid(
  object = workflow() |> 
    add_recipe(cherry_recipe) |> 
    add_model(lasso_tune_mod),
  resamples = folds, 
  grid = lasso_grid
)

rf_tune_res <- tune_race_anova(
  object = workflow() |>
      add_recipe(cherry_recipe) |>
      add_model(rf_tune_mod),
    resamples = folds,
    grid = rf_grid,
    control = control_race(),
    metrics = metric_set(mae)
  )

xgb_tune_res <- tune_race_anova(
  object = workflow() |>
      add_recipe(cherry_recipe) |>
      add_model(xgb_tune_mod),
    resamples = folds,
    grid = xgb_grid,
    control = control_race(),
    metrics = metric_set(mae)
  )

lgb_tune_res <- tune_race_anova(
  object = workflow() |>
      add_recipe(cherry_recipe) |>
      add_model(lgb_tune_mod),
    resamples = folds,
    grid = lgb_grid,
    control = control_race(),
    metrics = metric_set(mae)
  )

cub_tune_res <- tune_race_anova(
  object = workflow() |>
    add_recipe(cherry_recipe) |>
    add_model(cub_tune_mod),
  resamples = folds,
  grid = cub_grid,
  control = control_race(),
  metrics = metric_set(mae)
)
```

Use `finalize_workflow()` to fit the models with the best hyperparameter combination as assessed using k-fold cross validation to the whole training set.

```{r}
final_linear_fit <- fit(
  object = workflow() |>
      add_recipe(cherry_recipe) |>
      add_model(linear_mod), 
  data = data_train
  )

final_pca_fit <- fit(
  object = finalize_workflow(
      workflow() |>
      add_recipe(cherry_recipe) |>
      add_model(pca_tune_mod), 
      select_best(pca_tune_res)
      ), 
  data = data_train
  )

final_ridge_fit <- fit(
  object = finalize_workflow(
      workflow() |>
      add_recipe(cherry_recipe) |>
      add_model(ridge_tune_mod), 
      select_best(ridge_tune_res)
      ), 
  data = data_train
  )

final_lasso_fit <- fit(
  object = finalize_workflow(
      workflow() |>
      add_recipe(cherry_recipe) |>
      add_model(lasso_tune_mod), 
      select_best(lasso_tune_res)
      ), 
  data = data_train
  )

final_rf_fit <- fit(
  object = finalize_workflow(
      workflow() |>
      add_recipe(cherry_recipe) |>
      add_model(rf_tune_mod), 
      select_best(rf_tune_res)
      ), 
  data = data_train
  )

final_xgb_fit <- fit(
  object = finalize_workflow(
      workflow() |>
      add_recipe(cherry_recipe) |>
      add_model(xgb_tune_mod), 
      select_best(xgb_tune_res)
      ), 
  data = data_train
  )

final_lgb_fit <- fit(
  object = finalize_workflow(
      workflow() |>
      add_recipe(cherry_recipe) |>
      add_model(lgb_tune_mod), 
      select_best(lgb_tune_res)
      ), 
  data = data_train
  )

final_cub_fit <- fit(
  object = finalize_workflow(
    workflow() |>
      add_recipe(cherry_recipe) |>
      add_model(cub_tune_mod),
    select_best(cub_tune_res)
    ),
  data = data_train
  )
```

Evaluate the performance of the "final" model on the test set.

```{r}
final_linear_res <- predict(final_linear_fit, new_data = data_test) |> 
  bind_cols(data_test)

final_pca_res <- predict(final_pca_fit, new_data = data_test) |> 
  bind_cols(data_test)

final_ridge_res <- predict(final_ridge_fit, new_data = data_test) |> 
  bind_cols(data_test)

final_lasso_res <- predict(final_lasso_fit, new_data = data_test) |> 
  bind_cols(data_test)

final_rf_res <- predict(final_rf_fit, new_data = data_test) |> 
  bind_cols(data_test)

final_xgb_res <- predict(final_xgb_fit, new_data = data_test) |> 
  bind_cols(data_test)

final_lgb_res <- predict(final_lgb_fit, new_data = data_test) |> 
  bind_cols(data_test)

final_cub_res <- predict(final_cub_fit, new_data = data_test) |> 
  bind_cols(data_test)
```

Compute the mae for the "final" model. You can use the `{yardstick}` functions `mae()`.

```{r}
final_linear_mae <- mae(final_linear_res, truth = bloom_doy, estimate = .pred)

final_pca_mae <- mae(final_pca_res, truth = bloom_doy, estimate = .pred)

final_ridge_mae <- mae(final_ridge_res, truth = bloom_doy, estimate = .pred)

final_lasso_mae <- mae(final_lasso_res, truth = bloom_doy, estimate = .pred)

final_rf_mae <- mae(final_rf_res, truth = bloom_doy, estimate = .pred)

final_xgb_mae <- mae(final_xgb_res, truth = bloom_doy, estimate = .pred)

final_lgb_mae <- mae(final_lgb_res, truth = bloom_doy, estimate = .pred)

final_cub_mae <- mae(final_cub_res, truth = bloom_doy, estimate = .pred)

tribble(
  ~ model, ~ mae,
  "linear", final_linear_mae$.estimate,
  "pca", final_pca_mae$.estimate,
  "ridge", final_ridge_mae$.estimate,
  "lasso", final_lasso_mae$.estimate,
  "rf", final_rf_mae$.estimate,
  "xgb", final_xgb_mae$.estimate,
  "lgb", final_lgb_mae$.estimate,
  "cub", final_cub_mae$.estimate
  ) |> 
  arrange(mae)
```


```{r}
vip(final_rf_fit)
vip(final_lgb_fit)
vip(final_lgb_fit)
```



### Validation

The validation set is used to validate, and calibrate the models that were selected using k-fold CV and fitted on the whole training data set.

We use the `{probably}` package to add prediction intervals to our point forecasts.

Post-processing is important to handle any adjustments and bias for predictions.

We then use the calibrated models on our test dataset for a final evaluation.

Create the predictions for validation data

```{r}
rf_vpreds <- predict(rf_fit, validate)
lgb_vpreds <- predict(lgb_fit, validate)
cub_vpreds <- predict(cub_fit, validate)
```

Make a large dataframe with all predictions and the actual observations

```{r}
validate_preds <- validate |>
  cbind(
    rf = rf_vpreds$.pred,
    lgb = lgb_vpreds$.pred,
    cub = cub_vpreds$.pred
  ) |>
  relocate(year, location, bloom_doy, rf, lgb, cub) |> 
  pivot_longer(cols = c(rf, lgb, cub), names_to = "model", values_to = "value") |> 
  select(year, location, bloom_doy, model, value)
```

Visualize the certainty in predictions

```{r}
validate_preds |>
  ggplot(aes(x = bloom_doy, y = value, color = model)) +
  geom_point() +
  coord_equal() +
  geom_abline(lty = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(80, 110)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(80, 110)) +
  labs(
    title = "bloom_doy & predictions",
    x = "bloom_doy", y = "predictions"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Quick error measurement

```{r}
validate_preds |>
  mutate(abs_error = abs(bloom_doy - value)) |>
  group_by(model) |>
  summarize(avg_abs_error = mean(abs_error)) |> 
  arrange(avg_abs_error)
```

### Calibration

The top performing models on validation are cubist and random forest

Cubist is already pretty precise and accurate but we will calibrate our random forest to see if we increase accuracy on the validation set.

Calibrate random forest with validation data

```{r}
calibrate_rf <- data.frame(
  bloom_doy = validate$bloom_doy,
  .pred = rf_vpreds$.pred
)

rf_fit_cal <- calibrate_rf |>
  cal_estimate_linear(bloom_doy)

calibrated_rf_preds <- calibrate_rf |>
  cal_apply(rf_fit_cal)

calibrated_rf_preds |>
  mutate(abs_error = abs(bloom_doy - .pred)) |>
  summarize(avg_abs_error = mean(abs_error))
```

There is an improvement but note we need to **test** the calibration

### Intervals

While we have optimized our point forecasts with pre-processing, tuning, and post-processing, it's also important to capture our model uncertainty and to create robust prediction intervals with the validation set.

Let's create confidence intervals for our models. The simplest form being is the conformal split method implemented in the `{probably}` function `int_conformal_split()`.

```{r}
rf_int_model <- probably::int_conformal_split(rf_fit, validate)
lgb_int_model <- probably::int_conformal_split(lgb_fit, validate)
cub_int_model <- probably::int_conformal_split(cub_fit, validate)
```

We have obtained conformal interval models.

### Testing

We use the test data set to evaluate the performance of the models that we have trained on the test set and calibrated on the validation set.

Create the predictions and prediction intervals on the test set

```{r}
cubist_preds <- predict(cub_int_model, data_test, level = 0.90)

rf_cal_preds <- predict(rf_int_model, data_test, level = 0.90) |> 
  cal_apply(rf_fit_cal)

lgb_int_preds <- predict(lgb_int_model, data_test, level = 0.90)
```

Combine the test set and the predictions

```{r}
test_df <- data_test |>
  cbind(
    cubist = cubist_preds$.pred,
    cubist_upper = cubist_preds$.pred_upper,
    cubist_lower = cubist_preds$.pred_lower,
    rf_cal = rf_cal_preds$.pred,
    rf_cal_upper = rf_cal_preds$.pred_upper,
    rf_cal_lower = rf_cal_preds$.pred_lower,
    lgb = lgb_int_preds$.pred,
    lgb_upper = lgb_int_preds$.pred_upper,
    lgb_lower = lgb_int_preds$.pred_lower
  ) |> 
  select(year, location, bloom_doy, cubist, cubist_upper, cubist_lower, rf_cal, rf_cal_upper, rf_cal_lower, lgb, lgb_upper, lgb_lower)
```


```{r}
test_df |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(x = bloom_doy, y = bloom_doy, color = "actual")) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lgb_lower, xmax = lgb_upper, y = bloom_doy, color = "lgb_interval"), alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_point(aes(x = cubist, y = bloom_doy, color = "cubist")) +
  geom_point(aes(x = rf_cal, y = bloom_doy, color = "rf_calibrated")) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(80, 110)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(80, 110)) +
  geom_abline(lty = 2) +
  labs(x = "predictions", y = "bloom_doy") +
  theme_bw()
```
Test accuracy

```{r}
test_df |>
  mutate(
    cub_abs_error = abs(bloom_doy - cubist),
    rf_abs_error = abs(bloom_doy - rf_cal),
    lgb_coverage = ifelse(bloom_doy >= lgb_lower & bloom_doy <= lgb_upper, 1, 0),
    n = row_number()
  ) |>
  summarize(
    cub_total_abs_error = sum(cub_abs_error),
    rf_total_abs_error = sum(rf_abs_error),
    lgb_coverage_pct = sum(lgb_coverage) / max(n)
  )
```

## Submission

To submit your entries, enter the predicted bloom dates from your models in the **submission form**.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-predictions-for-submission
#| tbl-cap: "Predictions for Submission"

predictions |>
  filter(year == 2025) |>
  mutate(prediction_date = strptime(paste(year, prediction), "%Y %j") |> as_date()) |>
  kable() |> 
  kable_styling()
```

**NOTE**: The question is if we need to round the point estimates or if we can submit partial days.
